issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the other two memory items, which describe intrusive, sensory-dominated, repeatedly replaying trauma memories. That combination is not impossible, but with no other items indicating organized narrative access, the 'very easily' wording pulls in the opposite direction and is clinically inconsistent within this node.

issues.item: Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of mugging/robbery. 'Being around children' and 'Happy families' do not show a plausible thematic link to the reported trauma, and there are no accompanying threat or appraisal items to explain why these social/family cues would specifically trigger this patient's robbery-related PTSD.

issues.item: Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
issues.explanation: 'I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma' is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation mainly links triggers and memory with maladaptive strategies, but the actual triggers and memory content given are socially/family themed and intrusive-image based; deliberate conflict-seeking does not fit clearly with those items and looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, triggers centered on children and idealized families are hard to link clinically unless there is additional trauma meaning not represented elsewhere. The memory items describe perceptual re-experiencing of the robbery, but these triggers imply family/child themes that are absent from the rest of the profile, making the trigger set feel disconnected from the trauma type.

Within the Triggers node, 'children present' and 'happy families' suggest a loss/family-comparison theme, whereas 'being criticised or corrected' suggests interpersonal shame or sensitivity. These could coexist, but together they do not form a coherent trigger pattern tied to a robbery, especially given no threat or appraisal items supporting these meanings.

'Happy families' is a weakly plausible trigger for a mugging/robbery trauma and is hard to connect to the accompanying memory items, which are purely sensory/reliving-based and suggest trauma reminders tied more directly to the event. It does not fit well with the otherwise robbery-linked trigger pattern.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking conflict/create drama' is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The formulation links triggers and memory to maladaptive strategies, but the selected triggers and memory items imply intrusive re-experiencing, for which suppression/avoidance is coherent; deliberate conflict-seeking appears clinically disconnected and unusually externalising relative to the rest of the profile.

vignette: John is a 58-year-old African man who has been working as a hairdresser for over three decades. He married his high school sweetheart, and together they have raised two children now grown and out of the house. John's life took an abrupt turn one fateful evening last month when he was robbed outside his apartment building after work. On that night, John had just locked up his shop, a small salon in a busy strip mall where he has been working since his early twenties. The area around the strip mall is generally safe during the day but can be quieter and sparsely populated at night. As he was walking to his car parked on the other side of the building, John sensed someone behind him. Before he could turn around, a masked individual jumped out from the shadows, demanding his wallet. The attack was swift and brutal. The assailant knocked John to the ground and proceeded to rummage through his pockets. During the struggle, John's glasses were shattered, making it difficult for him to see or fight back effectively. He could feel the rough hands of the attacker, smell the strong scent of alcohol emanating from their breath, and hear the panicked beating of his own heart as he tried to protect himself. Since then, John has been plagued by vivid visual memories that replay over and over in his mind like a film. He knows what happened but struggles to find words to describe it fully, often feeling stuck in a loop of images and sensations from that night. The smell of alcohol now triggers intense distress, causing him to relive the fear and helplessness he felt during the mugging. John's work as a hairdresser has become particularly challenging since the event. He dreads going out alone at night and finds himself avoiding crowded areas where he might encounter suspicious-looking individuals. At his salon, he becomes increasingly agitated when clients make even minor criticisms or corrections about their hairstyles. What frightens him most is the fear of being caught off guard again by someone who seems to be acting suspiciously. To cope with these overwhelming feelings, John has adopted various maladaptive strategies. He often dwells on what he could have done differently that night and tries hard not to think about the trauma at all, burying his emotions deep down. This self-blame rumination leaves him feeling exhausted and isolated. He avoids social interactions and even begins to avoid people within his own community, fearing another encounter like the one outside his apartment. Over time, these avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on John's life. His marriage has suffered as he withdraws emotionally from his wife, who struggles to understand why her husband is no longer the person she once knew. In his salon, John's interactions with clients become tense and short-lived, leaving him feeling disconnected from what was once his passion. Despite these mounting difficulties, it wasn't until a close friend urged him to seek help that John finally decided to reach out for professional support. He knows he is struggling and fears becoming more isolated and unable to work or maintain relationships. What he hopes most for now is finding a way to reclaim some sense of normalcy in his life, to reconnect with the people around him without being haunted by the vivid memories of that fateful night. In therapy, John will need to navigate these complex emotions and maladaptive coping mechanisms while addressing the potent triggers linked directly to his traumatic experience. His journey towards recovery will involve understanding why these specific triggers are so powerful for him and learning healthier ways to cope with them without losing touch with himself or those he loves.
